questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $B=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{ln}⁡B.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and the given matrix $B,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡B=\operatorname{ln}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡D=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡1 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡B & =P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Block
questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{4}(1))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-3}} | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda =1.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} & -\frac{1}{{1}^{2}\cdot 2} & \frac{2}{{1}^{3}\cdot 6} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} & -\frac{1}{{1}^{2}\cdot 2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find ${2}^{A}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={2}^{x}$ and the given matrix $A,$ we have

$$
{2}^{A}={2}^{(PD{P}^{-1})}=P\cdot ({2}^{D})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
{2}^{D}=[\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{A} & =P\cdot ({2}^{D})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 4 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix
questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\pi ))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-4}} | $0$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡([\begin{aligned}{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(\pi )\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi ))\end{aligned}] \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(\pi ),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\pi )) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\pi )) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix
questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4}))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $2$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡([\begin{aligned}{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4}))\end{aligned}] \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
